name: Chemistry
note: Written for the 2017 Chemistry syllabus, which HSC 2027 and 2028 still use. Always check numbers and equations against your class notes.

cards.f: Define: static equilibrium.
cards.b: A system where forward and reverse reactions have stopped, e.g. a burnt match. Nothing is changing at the particle level.

cards.f: Define: dynamic equilibrium.
cards.b: A closed system where the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant while both reactions keep happening.

cards.f: What conditions are needed for a system to reach equilibrium?
cards.b: A closed system (no matter enters or leaves), a reversible reaction, and constant temperature.

cards.f: What is an open system versus a closed system?
cards.b: Open: matter and energy can be exchanged with the surroundings. Closed: energy can be exchanged but matter cannot.

cards.f: State Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.b: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the change, then reaches a new equilibrium.

cards.f: Effect of adding more reactant to a system at equilibrium?
cards.b: Equilibrium shifts right (forward reaction favoured) to use up some of the added reactant. K does not change.

cards.f: Effect of increasing pressure (reducing volume) on a gaseous equilibrium?
cards.b: Shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas, partially reducing the pressure. No effect if both sides have equal gas moles.

cards.f: Effect of increasing temperature on an exothermic equilibrium?
cards.b: Shifts left (endothermic reverse reaction favoured) to absorb heat. K decreases.

cards.f: Effect of increasing temperature on an endothermic equilibrium?
cards.b: Shifts right (forward reaction favoured) to absorb heat. K increases.

cards.f: Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium?
cards.b: None on position or K. It speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner.

cards.f: What is the only factor that changes the value of K?
cards.b: Temperature.

cards.f: Write the equilibrium expression for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD.
cards.b: K = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b, using equilibrium concentrations in mol/L. Pure solids and liquids are left out.

cards.f: What does a large K (K > 10^4) tell you?
cards.b: The equilibrium lies far to the right: products are strongly favoured.

cards.f: What does a small K (K < 10^-4) tell you?
cards.b: The equilibrium lies far to the left: reactants are strongly favoured.

cards.f: What is the reaction quotient Q and how is it used?
cards.b: Same expression as K but with current concentrations. Q < K: shifts right. Q > K: shifts left. Q = K: at equilibrium.

cards.f: Outline the cobalt chloride equilibrium.
cards.b: [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl4]2- (blue) + 6H2O. Endothermic forward: heating turns it blue, cooling turns it pink.

cards.f: Outline the NO2/N2O4 equilibrium.
cards.b: 2NO2 (brown) ⇌ N2O4 (colourless), exothermic forward. Heating gives a darker brown; increasing pressure first darkens then lightens as it shifts right.

cards.f: Outline the iron(III) thiocyanate equilibrium.
cards.b: Fe3+ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN2+ (blood red). Adding Fe3+ or SCN⁻ deepens the red; removing either fades it.

cards.f: Use collision theory to explain how equilibrium is reached.
cards.b: At first the forward rate is high. As reactant concentration falls and product rises, forward rate falls and reverse rate rises until they are equal.

cards.f: Define: enthalpy change (ΔH).
cards.b: Heat energy absorbed or released at constant pressure. Negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.

cards.f: Define: entropy (S).
cards.b: A measure of the disorder or number of ways energy and particles can be arranged. Gases > liquids > solids.

cards.f: State the Gibbs free energy equation and its meaning.
cards.b: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔG < 0 the reaction is spontaneous; if ΔG > 0 it is non-spontaneous; at ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

cards.f: Why does combustion not reach equilibrium?
cards.b: It is effectively irreversible: very exothermic, with a large increase in entropy, so ΔG is very negative and products escape in an open system.

cards.f: Why is photosynthesis non-spontaneous?
cards.b: ΔH is positive and entropy decreases, so ΔG > 0. It needs a continuous input of light energy.

cards.f: Define: solubility product (Ksp).
cards.b: The equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble salt dissolving, e.g. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag+][Cl⁻].

cards.f: How do you predict whether a precipitate forms?
cards.b: Calculate the ionic product Q with the mixed concentrations. If Q > Ksp a precipitate forms; if Q ≤ Ksp no precipitate.

cards.f: What is the common ion effect?
cards.b: Adding an ion already in a solubility equilibrium shifts it left, reducing the salt's solubility.

cards.f: Find the solubility s of a 1:1 salt from Ksp.
cards.b: Ksp = s², so s = √Ksp (mol/L).

cards.f: Find the solubility s of a 1:2 salt like PbCl2 from Ksp.
cards.b: Ksp = [Pb2+][Cl⁻]² = s(2s)² = 4s³, so s = ∛(Ksp/4).

cards.f: Outline how Aboriginal peoples removed toxins from cycad seeds.
cards.b: Seeds were crushed and leached in running water for days or weeks. The water-soluble toxin (cycasin) dissolved away, shifting it out of the seed.

cards.f: What are the solubility rules for nitrates, Group 1 and ammonium salts?
cards.b: Always soluble.

cards.f: Which common chlorides are insoluble?
cards.b: AgCl and PbCl2 (PbCl2 slightly soluble in hot water).

cards.f: Which common sulfates are insoluble or slightly soluble?
cards.b: BaSO4, PbSO4 and CaSO4 (slightly soluble), plus Ag2SO4 (slightly soluble).

cards.f: Which hydroxides are soluble?
cards.b: Group 1 hydroxides and Ba(OH)2. Ca(OH)2 is slightly soluble. Most others are insoluble.

cards.f: How does temperature affect K for an exothermic reaction? Give the evidence.
cards.b: K decreases as temperature increases, because the reverse endothermic reaction is favoured. Measured K values fall at higher temperatures.

cards.f: Define: Haber process equation and conditions.
cards.b: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. About 400–450 °C, 150–250 atm, iron catalyst: a compromise between yield and rate.

cards.f: Why is the Haber process run at a moderate temperature, not low?
cards.b: Low temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate. A moderate temperature with a catalyst gives an acceptable rate and yield.

cards.f: How do you calculate K from an ICE table?
cards.b: Write initial, change and equilibrium amounts using stoichiometry, convert to concentrations, then substitute into the K expression.

cards.f: Define an acid and a base (Arrhenius).
cards.b: Acid: produces H+ ions in water. Base: produces OH⁻ ions in water. Limited to aqueous solutions and can't explain basic NH3 or salts.

cards.f: Define an acid and a base (Brønsted–Lowry).
cards.b: Acid: proton (H+) donor. Base: proton acceptor. Works without water and explains NH3 and amphiprotic species.

cards.f: What is a conjugate acid–base pair?
cards.b: Two species that differ by one H+, e.g. NH4+/NH3 or H2O/OH⁻.

cards.f: Define: amphiprotic.
cards.b: A species that can donate or accept a proton, e.g. H2O, HCO3⁻, HSO4⁻, H2PO4⁻.

cards.f: Strong acid versus concentrated acid?
cards.b: Strong means it fully ionises in water. Concentrated means a large amount of acid per litre. A concentrated weak acid is possible.

cards.f: Name three strong acids.
cards.b: HCl, HNO3 and H2SO4 (first ionisation). Also HBr, HI and HClO4.

cards.f: Write the definition of pH and pOH.
cards.b: pH = −log[H+]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.

cards.f: What is Kw and its value at 25 °C?
What is Ka and what does a larger Ka mean?
cards.b: Ka = [H+][A⁻]/[HA] for a weak acid. A larger Ka (smaller pKa) means a stronger acid.

cards.f: How do you find pH of a weak acid from Ka?
cards.b: Assume [H+] = [A⁻] = x and [HA] ≈ initial c. Then x = √(Ka × c) and pH = −log x.

cards.f: Define pKa.
cards.b: pKa = −log Ka. Lower pKa means a stronger acid.

cards.f: What is neutralisation? Give the ionic equation.
cards.b: An acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water. Net ionic equation: H+ + OH⁻ → H2O.

cards.f: Is neutralisation exothermic or endothermic? Typical value?
cards.b: Exothermic. About −57 kJ per mole of water for a strong acid and strong base.

cards.f: Why is the enthalpy of neutralisation smaller for a weak acid?
cards.b: Some energy is used to ionise the weak acid fully as it reacts, so less heat is released overall.

cards.f: Acid + metal carbonate gives…?
cards.b: A salt, water and carbon dioxide, e.g. 2HCl + CaCO3 → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

cards.f: Acid + reactive metal gives…?
cards.b: A salt and hydrogen gas, e.g. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2.

cards.f: Define: primary standard. Give an example.
cards.b: A pure, stable, non-hygroscopic solid with a high molar mass, used to make a solution of exactly known concentration, e.g. anhydrous Na2CO3.

cards.f: Define: equivalence point versus end point.
cards.b: Equivalence point: moles of acid and base react in exact stoichiometric ratio. End point: where the indicator changes colour.

cards.f: Choose an indicator for strong acid / weak base titrations.
cards.b: Methyl orange (changes about pH 3.1–4.4) because the equivalence point is acidic.

cards.f: Choose an indicator for weak acid / strong base titrations.
cards.b: Phenolphthalein (changes about pH 8.3–10) because the equivalence point is basic.

cards.f: Why is the equivalence point basic for a weak acid / strong base titration?
cards.b: The conjugate base of the weak acid (e.g. CH3COO⁻) reacts with water to produce OH⁻.

cards.f: What should each piece of titration glassware be rinsed with?
cards.b: Burette and pipette: the solution they will hold. Conical flask: distilled water only.

cards.f: What is a conductometric titration?
cards.b: Following conductivity as titrant is added. The minimum or change in slope shows the equivalence point, because ions of different mobility replace each other.

cards.f: Define: buffer.
cards.b: A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.

cards.f: How does an ethanoic acid / ethanoate buffer work?
cards.b: Added H+ reacts with CH3COO⁻ to form CH3COOH. Added OH⁻ reacts with CH3COOH to form CH3COO⁻ and water. Equilibrium shifts limit the pH change.

cards.f: Name a natural buffer and where it acts.
cards.b: The carbonic acid/hydrogen carbonate (H2CO3/HCO3⁻) system in blood keeps pH about 7.35–7.45.

cards.f: Give a limitation of the Arrhenius model.
cards.b: It needs water, so it can't explain acid–base reactions in other solvents or gases (e.g. NH3 + HCl), or why NH3 is basic.

cards.f: Give a limitation of the Lavoisier and Davy models of acids.
cards.b: Lavoisier said acids contain oxygen (HCl has none). Davy said acids contain replaceable hydrogen, which didn't explain bases.

cards.f: Natural indicators: how is red cabbage used?
cards.b: Its anthocyanins change colour with pH: red in acid, purple near neutral, green to yellow in base.

cards.f: Calculate the pH of 0.010 mol/L HCl.
cards.b: Strong acid, so [H+] = 0.010, and pH = −log(0.010) = 2.00.

cards.f: Calculate the pH of 0.050 mol/L NaOH at 25 °C.
How do you find pH after mixing an acid and base?
cards.b: Find moles of H+ and OH⁻, subtract to find the excess, divide by the total volume, then calculate pH or pOH.

cards.f: Define: dilution formula.
cards.b: c1V1 = c2V2. Diluting a strong acid tenfold raises its pH by 1.

cards.f: What are acidic, basic and neutral salts?
cards.b: From a strong acid + weak base: acidic (NH4Cl). From a weak acid + strong base: basic (CH3COONa). From strong + strong: neutral (NaCl).

cards.f: What is a back titration and when is it used?
cards.b: Add a known excess of reagent, then titrate the leftover. Used for insoluble or volatile samples, e.g. CaCO3 in antacids.

cards.f: Define: hydrocarbon.
cards.b: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.

cards.f: Define: homologous series.
cards.b: A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH2, with gradually changing physical properties.

cards.f: General formulas: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes?
cards.b: Alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n-2.

cards.f: Define: structural isomers.
cards.b: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements: chain, position or functional group isomers.

cards.f: Name the functional group: R–OH.
cards.b: Hydroxyl: alcohol (suffix -ol).

cards.f: Name the functional group: R–COOH.
cards.b: Carboxyl: carboxylic acid (suffix -oic acid).

cards.f: Name the functional group: R–CHO and R–CO–R'.
cards.b: Aldehyde (-al, carbonyl at the end) and ketone (-one, carbonyl in the chain).

cards.f: Name the functional group: R–COO–R'.
cards.b: Ester (named alkyl alkanoate, e.g. ethyl ethanoate).

cards.f: Name the functional groups: amine and amide.
cards.b: Amine: –NH2 (suffix -amine). Amide: –CONH2 (suffix -amide).

cards.f: Why do boiling points rise along the alkanes?
cards.b: Longer chains have more electrons and surface area, so stronger dispersion forces.

cards.f: Why do alcohols boil higher than alkanes of similar mass?
cards.b: Alcohols form hydrogen bonds between –OH groups, which need more energy to overcome than dispersion forces.

cards.f: Why do carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass?
cards.b: They can form two hydrogen bonds per pair of molecules (dimers), and are more polar.

cards.f: Why are short alcohols water-soluble but long ones not?
cards.b: The –OH hydrogen bonds with water, but a long non-polar chain dominates, reducing solubility.

cards.f: Alkene + H2 (Ni catalyst) gives…?
cards.b: An alkane (hydrogenation).

cards.f: Alkene + Br2 gives…? Why is it a test?
cards.b: A dibromoalkane. Bromine water decolourises quickly with alkenes but not alkanes (which need UV light).

cards.f: Alkene + HX gives…?
cards.b: A haloalkane (hydrohalogenation).

cards.f: Alkene + water (acid catalyst) gives…?
cards.b: An alcohol (hydration), e.g. ethene + water → ethanol, with H3PO4 or dilute H2SO4.

cards.f: How do alkanes react with halogens?
cards.b: Substitution in UV light: an H is replaced by a halogen, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl.

cards.f: Primary alcohol + acidified K2Cr2O7 gives…?
cards.b: An aldehyde, then a carboxylic acid. The dichromate turns from orange to green.

cards.f: Secondary alcohol + acidified K2Cr2O7 gives…?
cards.b: A ketone. Orange to green.

cards.f: Tertiary alcohol + acidified K2Cr2O7?
cards.b: No reaction, so it stays orange.

cards.f: Define: dehydration of an alcohol.
cards.b: Heating with concentrated H2SO4 removes water to form an alkene.

cards.f: Outline esterification.
cards.b: Alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water, with concentrated H2SO4 catalyst, heated under reflux.

cards.f: Why is reflux used in esterification?
cards.b: Heating speeds the slow reaction while the condenser returns volatile reactants and products to the flask so nothing is lost.

cards.f: How is an ester purified after reflux?
cards.b: Wash with Na2CO3 solution in a separating funnel to remove acids, separate the layers, dry, then distil.

cards.f: Fermentation equation and conditions?
cards.b: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, with yeast, anaerobic, about 37 °C. Stops at about 15% ethanol.

cards.f: Compare fermentation and hydration of ethene for making ethanol.
cards.b: Fermentation: renewable but slow, batch, impure. Hydration: fast, continuous and pure, but uses non-renewable crude oil.

cards.f: Define: saponification.
cards.b: Heating a fat (triglyceride) with NaOH to produce glycerol and soap (sodium salts of fatty acids).

cards.f: How do soaps clean?
cards.b: The non-polar hydrocarbon tail dissolves in grease and the ionic head faces the water, forming micelles that lift the grease off.

cards.f: Soap versus detergent?
cards.b: Detergents are synthetic. Many still work in hard water, because their ionic heads don't form precipitates with Ca2+ and Mg2+.

cards.f: Name the three types of detergents.
cards.b: Anionic (e.g. sulfonates), cationic (e.g. quaternary ammonium) and non-ionic (e.g. polyethoxylates).

cards.f: Define: addition polymer. Example?
cards.b: A polymer made by joining alkene monomers by breaking C=C bonds, with no other product, e.g. polyethylene from ethene.

cards.f: LDPE versus HDPE?
cards.b: LDPE: branched chains, low density, flexible (plastic bags). HDPE: unbranched, closely packed, stronger and denser (bottles, pipes).

cards.f: Name the monomers of PVC, polystyrene and PTFE.
cards.b: Chloroethene (vinyl chloride), styrene (phenylethene) and tetrafluoroethene.

cards.f: Define: condensation polymer. Two examples?
cards.b: Monomers join and release a small molecule such as water. Polyesters (e.g. PET) and polyamides (e.g. nylon).

cards.f: Name the IUPAC rules in order.
cards.b: Find the longest chain with the functional group, number it to give the functional group the lowest number, then name and number the branches alphabetically.

cards.f: Define: complete combustion of an alkane.
cards.b: Alkane + oxygen → CO2 + H2O, releasing lots of energy. Incomplete combustion makes CO and/or soot.

cards.f: What does an enthalpy of combustion experiment measure?
cards.b: Heat absorbed by water: q = mcΔT, divided by moles of fuel burnt. Results are lower than data values because of heat loss and incomplete combustion.

cards.f: Flame test colours: Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cu2+, Ba2+?
cards.b: Na+ yellow-orange, K+ lilac, Ca2+ brick red, Cu2+ blue-green, Ba2+ pale green (apple green).

cards.f: Test for Cl⁻ ions?
cards.b: Add dilute HNO3 then AgNO3: a white precipitate of AgCl that darkens in light.

cards.f: Test for SO4 2- ions?
cards.b: Add dilute HCl then BaCl2 (or Ba(NO3)2): a white precipitate of BaSO4.

cards.f: Test for CO3 2- ions?
cards.b: Add dilute acid: bubbles of CO2 that turn limewater milky.

cards.f: Test for Fe3+ ions?
cards.b: Add KSCN: a blood-red colour (FeSCN2+). Or NaOH gives a red-brown precipitate.

cards.f: Test for Fe2+ ions?
cards.b: NaOH gives a green precipitate of Fe(OH)2.

cards.f: Test for Cu2+ ions?
cards.b: NaOH gives a pale blue precipitate. Adding excess NH3 gives a deep blue solution.

cards.f: Test for Ba2+ and Pb2+?
cards.b: Ba2+: add H2SO4 for a white precipitate. Pb2+: add KI for a bright yellow precipitate of PbI2.

cards.f: What is gravimetric analysis?
cards.b: Precipitating an ion as an insoluble compound, filtering, drying to constant mass and weighing it to work out the amount of the ion.

cards.f: How does atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) work?
cards.b: A lamp of the target element shines through the atomised sample. Absorbance is proportional to concentration, read from a calibration curve.

cards.f: What is a calibration curve?
cards.b: A graph of absorbance against concentration for standard solutions, used to find an unknown's concentration from its absorbance.

cards.f: What is the Beer–Lambert law in words?
cards.b: Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration, at a fixed wavelength and path length.

cards.f: What does UV-visible spectrophotometry measure?
cards.b: Absorption of UV or visible light by coloured or conjugated compounds, to find concentration using a calibration curve.

cards.f: Test for an alkene?
cards.b: Bromine water decolourises rapidly (orange to colourless) with no UV light needed.

cards.f: Test for an alcohol?
cards.b: Acidified dichromate turns orange to green for primary and secondary alcohols. Sodium metal produces H2 gas.

cards.f: Test for a carboxylic acid?
cards.b: Add Na2CO3 or NaHCO3: fizzing of CO2. It also turns blue litmus red.

cards.f: What does mass spectrometry tell you?
cards.b: The molecular mass from the molecular ion (M+) peak, and structure clues from fragment peaks, e.g. m/z 15 = CH3+.

cards.f: What does infrared spectroscopy tell you?
cards.b: Which functional groups are present from bond vibrations, e.g. broad O–H about 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, C=O about 1700 cm⁻¹.

cards.f: What does 13C NMR tell you?
cards.b: The number of different carbon environments (number of peaks) and their type from the chemical shift.

cards.f: What does 1H NMR tell you?
cards.b: The number of hydrogen environments (peaks), how many H in each (integration) and neighbouring H (splitting, n + 1 rule).

cards.f: State the n + 1 rule.
cards.b: A proton signal splits into n + 1 peaks, where n is the number of H atoms on neighbouring carbons.

cards.f: Broad IR peak at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ plus a peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ suggests…?
cards.b: A carboxylic acid (O–H of the acid plus C=O).

cards.f: What is the role of TMS in NMR?
cards.b: Tetramethylsilane is the reference compound, set at a chemical shift of 0 ppm.

cards.f: Outline a chemical synthesis process to evaluate.
cards.b: Consider yield, rate, cost of reactants, energy use, waste and by-products, safety and environmental impact.

cards.f: Why are some reactions monitored by chemists in industry?
cards.b: To keep yield, purity and safety high, minimise waste and cost, and meet environmental standards.

cards.f: Why is it important to analyse soil and water for heavy metals?
cards.b: Heavy metals such as Pb, Hg and Cd are toxic, bioaccumulate in food chains and harm health even at low concentrations.

cards.f: What is a precipitation titration? Example?
cards.b: A titration where the product is a precipitate, e.g. Mohr method: Ag+ titrated against Cl⁻ using a chromate indicator.

cards.f: Identify: m/z peak at 29 in a mass spectrum.
cards.b: Often CHO+ or C2H5+ fragments.

cards.f: How do you combine spectra to identify a compound?
cards.b: Mass spec gives the molar mass, IR gives the functional groups, 13C NMR gives the carbon environments and 1H NMR gives H environments and neighbours.

cards.f: Why use more than one analytical technique?
cards.b: Each gives partial information. Combining them confirms the structure and reduces errors from any one method.
